title: Steak and Mushroom Pie
subtitle: Chuck steak braised with chestnut mushrooms and red wine under a puff pastry lid
excerpt: Steak and mushroom pie swaps the kidney for chestnut mushrooms, making a gentler but still deeply savoury pie that suits those who prefer to leave organ meat aside. The beef is braised with red wine until tender, the sauce is reduced to a glossy gravy, and the whole thing is topped with a golden puff pastry lid.
sourceNotes: Adapted from the classic British braised-beef pie tradition. Chestnut mushroom and red wine variation is modern British home cooking, drawing on the steak and ale method from Isabella Beeton (1836 to 1865), the Victorian household writer, (Project Gutenberg #10136) with the ale replaced by red wine.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the assembled unbaked pie for up to 2 months. Bake from frozen at 180°C for 50 to 60 minutes, covering loosely if the pastry colours too quickly.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Cool fully before topping with pastry.

content.text: Steak and mushroom pie has a puff pastry lid over a braised beef and mushroom filling. The mushrooms add body and a deeper, earthier note than a plain beef gravy. It is one of the more forgiving British pies to make at home: puff pastry from a packet, the filling braised in one pot, the assembly taking ten minutes.
Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven over high heat. Pat the beef dry and brown in batches until deep brown on all sides, about 3 to 4 minutes per batch. Set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onions and cook for 8 minutes until softened. Add the crushed garlic and cook for 1 minute. Sprinkle over the flour and stir well to coat the onions.

Return the beef to the pan. Pour in the red wine, let it bubble for 2 minutes, then add the beef stock and the tomato purée. Add the thyme sprigs. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook on a low heat for 1 hour 20 minutes.
Add the mushrooms, cover, and cook for a further 20 minutes. Remove the lid and cook for 10 more minutes to reduce the gravy slightly. Remove the thyme. Taste and season. Cool completely.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Spoon the cooled filling into a deep pie dish or casserole. Unroll the pastry and lay it over the dish, pressing to the rim. Trim the overhang to about 1 cm and crimp or press with a fork to seal.
Cut two small slits in the top for steam to escape. Brush with beaten egg. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the pastry is well risen and deeply golden.

items.cause: The filling was still warm when the pastry was laid on
items.fix: Always cool the filling completely: or refrigerate it: before covering with pastry. Heat softens the fat in puff pastry before it goes into the oven.

items.cause: The pastry was stretched or pressed down too hard onto the rim
items.fix: Rest the pastry over the filling loosely: don't stretch it. Press the edge to the rim but don't flatten the layers of pastry above the filling itself.

items.cause: The gravy was not reduced before assembling
items.fix: After removing the lid in the final stage, simmer uncovered for longer until the gravy coats the back of a spoon. A thin filling makes for a wet crust.

items.cause: The heat was too high and the liquid reduced before the collagen in the chuck broke down
items.fix: Top up with 100 ml more stock, cover again, and continue at a lower heat. Chuck needs gentle, consistent heat to become tender.

content.text: The mushroom version of the British beef pie became the standard weeknight variant once kidney fell out of fashion with younger cooks. It keeps all the structural logic of the original: braised chuck, dark gravy, pastry lid: and adds a meatier body through the mushrooms. It is the version you find in most British pub pubs today and in most home kitchens with children to feed.
